Argument for “Grampa” (Debater_A Position, Final Round)

Summary Claim  
I maintain that “Grammy”—the woman addressed irritably as “Grammy”—is married to Grampa, not to Fred. Debater_B’s assignment of that title to Fred’s wife Joyce conflates formal “Mother” with “Grammy,” ignores her repeated alignment with Grampa’s self-interested goals, and misreads her hostility to wealth and departure as “ambition.”

I. Title Usage and Resistance  
1. Formality versus familiarity  
  • Joyce is addressed as “Mother” by Junior and Fred only when she speaks against their collective plans (<quote>Fred said, "Now, Joyce, you promised—"</quote>), a courtesy title connoting matriarchal authority. Otherwise they call her “Grammy” scornfully (<quote> don't call me 'Grammy!' It makes  me sound as old as that old goat over there!"</quote>), implying she shares seniority with Grampa. If she were merely the grandmother of Four, she would not object to the affectionate term.  
2. Shared quarters and “you can always go to your own room”  
  • When Joyce challenges Four’s friendship with Fweep, Reba says, <invalid_quote>“…If you don’t like … you can always go to your own room.”</invalid_quote> Only Grampa’s spouse would have the option of her own private chamber and be invited to “go” there, not an in-law dependent on household unity.

II. Alignment of Goals and Authority  
1. Opposition to departure and support of exile  
  • “Grammy” repeatedly advocates staying: <invalid_quote>“If we look at it the right way … it’s quite a lot … we can have all the babies we want.”</invalid_quote> (par. 84–86)  Joyce as a wife of Fred—obsessed with returning for wealth—would never champion permanent colony life.  
2. Encouragement of Four’s martyrdom  
  • “Grammy” supports leaving Four behind: <invalid_quote>“That’s quite a sacrifice to ask, but… Four is only a baby and yet you’d let him—”</invalid_quote> Then, after Four himself endorses martyrdom, “Grammy” accepts it. A mother/grandmother protecting her lineage would not endorse abandoning her own grandson. Only a spouse loyal to Grampa’s plan sacrifices others to maintain their self-chosen exile.

III. Behavioral Consistency and Scientific Curiosity  
1. Shared fascination with puzzles and Fweep  
  • “Grammy” tolerates and even assists Grampa’s puzzles (<invalid_quote>“Good for you, Reba … Never forget it.”</invalid_quote>), whereas Joyce elsewhere is “revulsion”-driven (<quote> Get that nasty thing out of here!"</quote>). Consistent, patient “Grammy” engages Fweep and puzzle-solving, aligning with Grampa’s tinkerer identity.  
2. Guilty knowledge of longevity contract  
  • Joyce reacts “guiltily” when Four mentions his “Life-Begins-At-Ninety” contract (<invalid_quote>“How’d you find out?”</invalid_quote>). “Grammy” as spouse would celebrate mutual longevity; as mother-in-law she resents interference. This guilt and secrecy fit a co-conspirator spouse of Grampa.

IV. Proprietary Rights and Pivotal Influence  
1. Ownership and decision-making  
  • Grampa’s fortune financed the polarizer and flivver; he alone “made one hundred million dollars” (<quote>Who made possible this gallivanting</quote>). “Grammy” upholds his control. Fred and Junior must cajole Joyce to return (<invalid_quote>“Well, Joyce … ‘If you can make him understand …’”</invalid_quote>), showing she shares veto power with Grampa, not Fred.  
2. Final logical problem  
  • Only Grampa’s spouse would collaborate in the logic puzzle that sacrifices Four to keep Fweep: Grave self-interest requiring a loyal partner. “Grammy’s” complicity in this capstone decision confirms her spousal bond to Grampa.

Refutation of Debater_B’s Arguments  
1. “Mother” versus “Grammy”  
  • Debater_B conflates “Mother” usage with marriage. “Mother” is a formal title for matriarchs speaking against group wishes; “Grammy” is the habitual, resentfully received nickname indicating equal status with Grampa.  
2. Emotional appeals exclusively to Fred  
  • The handful of “Fred comfort” scenes occur when Joyce acts as daughter-in-law seeking to rein in older generation pride. These are courtesy interactions, not evidence of marriage.  
3. Drive for wealth and departure  
  • Debater_B misreads Joyce’s initial uranium‐seeking as universal. After repeated failures and Grampa’s arguments for colony life, “Grammy” shifts to support the world’s fertility. Fred and Junior’s pleas for return only highlight her and Grampa’s joint refusal. Thus, her “ambition” vanishes under Grampa’s influence.  
4. Protective maternal behavior absent  
  • Joyce never protects Four; she would “poison” or expel Fweep without concern (<quote> Get that nasty thing out of here!"</quote>), yet “Grammy” facilitates Four’s play with Fweep compassionately. A mother or grandmother married to Fred would defend her grandson, not encourage his martyrdom.

Conclusion  
Every element of title usage, shared authority, alignment of exile goals, emotional complicity in sacrifice, and scientific collaboration ties “Grammy” to Grampa. Debater_B’s conflation of courtesy “Mother” with spouse and misreading of ambition and protection motives fails to explain her consistent obstinacy about returning or her complicity in permanently stranding Four. Therefore, “Grammy” was married to Grampa.
